ideas.hypothesis: The extreme right tail of annual per-person health care costs is driven largely by end-of-life care. Measuring costs in life-years before death rather than calendar years, and conditioning on time-to-death, will substantially reduce the estimated tail index and the share of spending held by the top 1%.
ideas.test: Individual-level claims with death dates (e.g., a national insurer extract or a Medicare 5% sample). Estimate the Hill tail index and top-1% spending share for the full population, then with decedents excluded and with time-to-death indicators added, comparing calendar-year and life-year cost definitions.
ideas.disconfirming: The tail index and top-1% concentration stay essentially unchanged after removing decedents or conditioning on time-to-death.

ideas.hypothesis: Skewness and the variance-to-mean relationship of per-patient melanoma costs rise with clinical stage. As a result, estimators that assume one variance function across stages (OLS on raw costs, or a single GLM family) misestimate stage III-IV excess costs.
ideas.test: Registry-linked direct cost data for melanoma patients by stage (Swedish county data as in the source). Fit OLS, log-OLS with smearing, gamma GLM and extended estimating equations. Run a modified Park test by stage, then compare out-of-sample prediction error by stage.
ideas.disconfirming: The variance-function parameter is the same across stages, and all estimators give similar stage-specific means and prediction errors.

ideas.hypothesis: Moving a share of deaths from hospital to home or long-term care settings saves less than commonly assumed, because higher long-term care costs in the last year of life offset much of the avoided acute care cost.
ideas.test: A decision model calibrated to Dutch last-year-of-life cure and care costs by place of death. Run what-if scenarios shifting 10-30% of hospital deaths to other settings, with probabilistic sensitivity analysis.
ideas.disconfirming: Scenarios show savings that scale with avoided inpatient costs, with little offset from long-term care.

ideas.hypothesis: Melanoma patients with comorbid diagnosed depression have higher stage-adjusted direct costs than other patients. The relative cost increase is largest at early stages, where baseline treatment costs are low.
ideas.test: A cancer-registry cohort linked to outpatient and inpatient cost records and to depression diagnoses or antidepressant prescriptions. Fit a gamma GLM of two-year direct costs on depression, stage and their interaction, with age and sex controls.
ideas.disconfirming: Depression has no significant cost effect after stage adjustment, or the relative increase is the same across stages.

ideas.hypothesis: Giving patients provider-specific price information lowers spending on shoppable services more for high-deductible plan enrollees than for traditional plan enrollees, because the deductible makes the information matter to their own payments.
ideas.test: Employer claims data spanning the staggered rollout of a price-transparency tool. Run a triple difference (tool access x HDHP x post period) on prices paid for imaging and lab services.
ideas.disconfirming: The tool's effect on prices paid is the same or smaller for HDHP enrollees.

ideas.hypothesis: Insurers in more competitive markets with higher enrollee churn are less likely to use cost-effectiveness evidence in coverage decisions, because they keep a smaller share of long-run savings.
ideas.test: Code a sample of insurer coverage policies for explicit citation of CEA or ICER thresholds. Link to market-level insurer HHI and enrollee churn rates and estimate a logit of CEA use.
ideas.disconfirming: CEA use is unrelated to churn or competition, or is higher in more competitive, high-churn markets.

ideas.hypothesis: Health systems with long beneficiary enrollment horizons, such as the military and veterans systems, tie formulary restrictiveness to cost-effectiveness more closely than commercial managed care organizations do.
ideas.test: For a set of drugs with published ICERs, collect formulary status and restrictions from the veterans/military formulary and from several large commercial plans. Compare the correlation between ICER and restrictiveness across payer types.
ideas.disconfirming: The ICER-restrictiveness correlation is no stronger, or is weaker, for the long-horizon systems.

ideas.hypothesis: Warranty-style reimbursement, where providers absorb the cost of defects, works as a quality signal. Where public quality information is scarce, hospitals offering warranties gain market share for the covered procedures.
ideas.test: All-payer discharge data for a warranty-eligible procedure (e.g., CABG or joint replacement) before and after some hospitals adopt warranties. Run difference-in-differences on market share, interacted with whether a public report card exists in the market.
ideas.disconfirming: Warranty adopters gain no market share, or gain more where public quality information is abundant.

ideas.hypothesis: Episode payments that make providers bear complication costs for cancer surgery reduce 90-day readmissions and the variance of post-surgical costs, with only a small rise in index-admission costs.
ideas.test: Compare cancer surgery episodes under a bundled or warranty pilot with matched fee-for-service episodes. Outcomes are 90-day total cost, cost variance, readmissions and index costs.
ideas.disconfirming: Complication-related costs do not fall, or are fully offset by higher index costs.

ideas.hypothesis: Introducing DRG payment shortens terminal hospital stays and moves end-of-life spending from acute inpatient care to long-term and home care, so total last-year-of-life costs barely change.
ideas.test: Interrupted time series of decedents' last-year costs by sector, before and after DRG introduction in Austria (1997), with a non-DRG comparison country or region.
ideas.disconfirming: Total last-year costs fall significantly, or no shift between sectors appears.

ideas.hypothesis: Women's last-year-of-life costs lean more toward long-term care and men's toward acute care. The gap shrinks substantially once age at death and living arrangement (e.g., widowhood) are adjusted for.
ideas.test: Registry data on decedents' cure and care costs. Estimate gender-stratified structural models of cost composition with and without age at death and household status.
ideas.disconfirming: There is no gender gap in composition, or it persists unchanged after adjustment.

ideas.hypothesis: Patients attributed to ACOs are diagnosed with cancer at earlier stages, which lowers first-year cancer care costs through stage mix rather than through lower prices.
ideas.test: Registry-claims linked data (e.g., SEER-Medicare). Run difference-in-differences on stage at diagnosis and first-year costs for ACO-attributed versus non-attributed beneficiaries around ACO entry, then decompose cost changes into stage-mix and within-stage components.
ideas.disconfirming: There is no stage shift, or ACO cost differences are entirely within-stage.

ideas.hypothesis: Public willingness to share the costs of treatment falls more when illness is attributed to alcohol use than to other behaviors. The penalty shrinks when the drinking is framed as a mental health condition.
ideas.test: An online vignette experiment with a national sample. Randomize the stated cause of illness (alcohol, diet, inborn) and the framing (behavior vs. disorder), and measure support for public payment.
ideas.disconfirming: Support does not differ by alcohol attribution, or the framing has no effect.

ideas.hypothesis: Regions with higher per-capita spending on mental health services have lower years of life lost from suicide and substance-related causes, after adjusting for confounders.
ideas.test: Regional panel of mental health spending and cause-specific YLL (e.g., Austrian or Dutch regions over 10+ years), with region and year fixed effects and socioeconomic controls.
ideas.disconfirming: There is no association, or a positive one, between mental health spending and cause-specific YLL.

ideas.hypothesis: Integrating behavioral health into primary care lowers total health care costs more for heavy drinkers than for other patients.
ideas.test: Integrated health-system EHR and claims data with staggered rollout of embedded behavioral clinicians. Run a triple difference by baseline alcohol screening score on total costs.
ideas.disconfirming: Cost reductions are no larger for heavy drinkers.

ideas.hypothesis: Markets where a larger share of payments runs through value-based contracts see more entry of new provider organization types than markets dominated by volume-based payment.
ideas.test: County-level panel of new provider organization registrations from national provider registries, linked to the share of beneficiaries in alternative payment models. Use fixed-effects regression.
ideas.disconfirming: Entry is unrelated to, or lower with, value-based payment penetration.

ideas.hypothesis: The marginal reduction in years of life lost for each extra unit of health spending is larger for men than for women, consistent with the gender differences in health care use processes.
ideas.test: Re-estimate a regional spending-outcome panel with gender-specific YLL as outcomes and test whether the spending coefficients differ.
ideas.disconfirming: The spending elasticities are equal, or larger for women.

ideas.hypothesis: Across OECD countries, the ratio of decedent to survivor spending is higher in hospital-centric systems, and this ratio explains part of the cross-country variation in total health spending.
ideas.test: Compile decedent-to-survivor cost ratios from national studies for 10-15 OECD countries. Regress per-capita spending on the ratio and on hospital beds per capita.
ideas.disconfirming: The decedent cost ratio is unrelated to hospital orientation or to total spending.

ideas.hypothesis: Growth in the number of cancer survivors accounts for a measurable share of per-capita spending growth, while quality-adjusted price indexes for cancer episodes rise more slowly than unadjusted cost per patient.
ideas.test: Decompose regional spending growth into survivor prevalence and cost per patient. Build a cost-of-treatment index for melanoma episodes, adjusted for survival gains.
ideas.disconfirming: Survivor prevalence explains a negligible share of growth, and quality-adjusted and unadjusted indexes move together.

ideas.hypothesis: Adding EHR-derived clinical measures (labs, vitals, functioning scores) to claims-based risk adjustment improves prediction of top-percentile costs much more than prediction of mean costs.
ideas.test: Integrated delivery-system data with both claims and EHR fields. Compare claims-only and claims+EHR models on predictive ratios for the top 1% and on overall R-squared in a holdout sample.
ideas.disconfirming: The EHR variables improve tail prediction no more than mean prediction.

ideas.hypothesis: Under single-payer provincial systems, centralized drug review reduces variation across provinces in new-drug listing decisions and time to listing.
ideas.test: Provincial formulary listing dates for new drugs before and after the Common Drug Review began (2003). Compare the cross-provincial dispersion of listing status and time to listing.
ideas.disconfirming: Cross-provincial variation does not decline after centralized review.

ideas.hypothesis: After Canada centralized drug reimbursement review, the Canada-US gap in per-capita prescription drug spending widened, beyond what utilization differences explain.
ideas.test: Interrupted time series of per-capita drug spending in both countries, 1995-2015, with a break at 2003 and controls for prescription volume.
ideas.disconfirming: The gap's trend does not change after 2003.

ideas.hypothesis: Moving Medicaid enrollees into risk-based managed care lowers amenable years of life lost in low-income populations by improving primary care access.
ideas.test: Staggered county-level adoption of mandatory Medicaid managed care. Run difference-in-differences on amenable-cause YLL from vital statistics.
ideas.disconfirming: Amenable YLL does not change, or rises, after the transition.

ideas.hypothesis: Lower-SES decedents incur lower acute care costs but higher long-term care costs in their last year of life than higher-SES decedents, so total costs vary less by SES than their composition does.
ideas.test: Registry data on decedents' costs linked to income or education. Regress acute and long-term care costs on SES, controlling for age, sex and cause of death.
ideas.disconfirming: There is no SES gradient in cost composition.

ideas.hypothesis: Attributing depression to inborn biological causes rather than individual behavior raises public support for publicly financed mental health care.
ideas.test: A survey vignette experiment that randomizes the stated cause of a depression case and measures support for covering treatment costs.
ideas.disconfirming: Support does not differ by causal attribution.

ideas.hypothesis: During economic downturns, growth in pharmaceutical spending slows less than growth in hospital spending, so drugs take a larger share of health spending.
ideas.test: OECD-country panel of spending components, 2000-2015, regressed on recession indicators and output gaps, with country fixed effects.
ideas.disconfirming: Drug spending falls as much as, or more than, hospital spending during downturns.

ideas.hypothesis: Higher midlife alcohol consumption predicts higher long-term care costs in old age, mediated by decline in physical functioning, with stronger mediation in men.
ideas.test: Longitudinal cohort with baseline alcohol measures linked to later long-term care claims. Fit gender-stratified structural equation models with functioning as mediator.
ideas.disconfirming: Alcohol consumption has no association with long-term care costs after controls, or no mediation through functioning.

ideas.hypothesis: Chronic disease management programs reduce the upper tail of the cost distribution (90th-99th percentiles) more than mean costs.
ideas.test: Claims data for enrollees and matched non-enrollees in a disease management program. Run quantile difference-in-differences at the 50th, 90th and 99th percentiles of annual cost.
ideas.disconfirming: Effects are concentrated at the median or are uniform across quantiles.

ideas.hypothesis: Nonprofit hospitals that sharply raise capital spending on ACO-related infrastructure reduce charity care relative to peers.
ideas.test: Hospital panel linking capital expenditures from cost reports to charity care from community benefit filings. Use fixed-effects regression around ACO participation.
ideas.disconfirming: Charity care is unchanged or rises with capital spending increases.

ideas.hypothesis: Regions with higher penetration of capitated managed care show slower health spending growth with no increase in risk-adjusted mortality.
ideas.test: State- or region-level panel of capitation penetration, per-capita spending growth and age-adjusted mortality, with fixed effects.
ideas.disconfirming: Mortality rises with capitation penetration, or spending growth does not slow.
